headline: New members join. Budgets expand. Tests delay.
deck: This week, the space industry sees new entrants, budget boosts, and persistent testing woes.

stories.head: Commercial Space Federation adds semiconductor flair
stories.body: The Commercial Space Federation has welcomed Besxar and Charter Space, both adding semiconductor expertise to the supply chain. This move aims to enhance the resilience and efficiency of space operations, particularly in satellite manufacturing. With semiconductors being crucial for modern technology, their inclusion signals a strategic shift towards integrating more advanced tech into the aerospace ecosystem.
stories.soWhat: In a space race where chips are the new gold, these additions might just be the boost the industry needs to stay competitive.

stories.head: Spire teams with Diehl for missile warning tech
stories.body: Spire has partnered with German defense firm Diehl Defence to explore space-based missile warning capabilities. This collaboration comes at a time when global defense needs are evolving, and the demand for advanced surveillance systems is on the rise. The financial terms of the partnership haven't been disclosed, but it positions Spire as a player in the critical defense sector.
stories.soWhat: If Spire can deliver, they might just redefine the boundaries of what commercial space firms can do in the defense arena.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M, eyes co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly has successfully closed a $190 million Series C funding round, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion. The company focuses on co-orbital security and space domain awareness, tapping into the growing demand for defense capabilities in space. With this funding, True Anomaly is set to enhance its technology and potentially reshape the security landscape in low Earth orbit.
stories.soWhat: When it comes to space security, cash is king, and True Anomaly just bought a bigger crown.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
